videos.title: The Placebo Effect, Explained in 60 Seconds
videos.hook: Why does your mind sometimes trick your body into feeling better or worse?
videos.topic: The placebo effect explained in 60 seconds (follow-up to our 'drunk on zero alcohol' Short): open by saying 'The placebo effect is when believing something will affect you makes your body and brain react as if it really did.' Then 3 quick real examples: sugar pills that make patients feel better because they expect them to work; the 2003 Assefi and Garry study where students drinking plain tonic they thought was vodka acted drunk; and how expecting to do badly makes people perform worse. End with how to use it for confidence: what you expect of yourself shapes how you act. Keep it clear and teaching-first, not a long story || Title: The Placebo Effect, Explained in 60 Seconds

videos.title: The Placebo Effect: They Got Drunk on Drinks With Zero Alcohol
videos.hook: Why does a glass of water taste like vodka when you think it does?
videos.topic: The placebo effect: people got drunk on drinks with zero alcohol. Real study: in 2003 Seema Assefi and Maryanne Garry (published in Psychological Science) gave 148 students plain tonic water; half were told it was vodka and tonic. The tonic was poured from real vodka bottles and the glass rims were wiped with limes dipped in vodka. The 'vodka' group acted drunk, some showed physical signs of being drunk, and many insisted they had felt drunk when told the truth. They were also easier to mislead in a memory test, and more confident in their wrong memories. Lesson: what you believe changes how you act, so your beliefs about yourself (confidence, money, ability) work the same way. Do not claim they slurred their words || Title: The Placebo Effect: They Got Drunk on Drinks With Zero Alcohol
